title: Homilies on the Gospel of John
subtitle: Selections from the eighty-eight homilies
source: Summarized from Schaff, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Volume 14 (1889), public domain. Marginal notes by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: Why John speaks so high
paragraphs: Chrysostom preached eighty-eight homilies on the Fourth Gospel to the congregation of Antioch around the year 391. In the opening homilies he asks why the Spirit had John, the unschooled fisherman of Galilee, speak the most exalted theology the world has ever heard. His answer is a contrast: the philosophers and rhetoricians of Greece had labored for centuries with brilliant minds and produced systems that contradicted each other within a generation. John spoke the truth about God once and for all, and the world's wisdom has not been able to overturn it.

Chrysostom dwells on the phrase 'In the beginning was the Word.' He notes the carefully chosen verb. The evangelist does not say 'the Word came to be' or 'God made the Word,' as Moses said God made the heaven and the earth. He says 'the Word was,' and the imperfect tense is open-ended in both directions. As far back as you push your mind, the Word was already there. This is the answer to the Arian claim that 'there was when He was not.' There was no such moment.
notes: Chrysostom's argument here is the same one his fellow Antiochene, Athanasius before him, and his contemporary Gregory the Theologian had to make against the Arian school. The Gospel of John is the patristic battlefield where the Nicene faith was won.
The Antioch congregation Chrysostom preached to was largely literate and used to long oration; the homilies as we have them are heavily verbal and meant to be heard aloud, not silently read.

sections.title: The bread of life
paragraphs: In Homily 46 Chrysostom takes up the sixth chapter of John, where Christ promises His own flesh as the food that gives eternal life. He is direct where some later Western teachers would grow cautious. The bread, he says, is the very Body of Christ; the cup is the very Blood. The believer who receives them receives the Lord, not a symbol of the Lord.

Chrysostom asks why Christ gave us so great a mystery in so plain a form. His answer is that the Lord knows our weakness. We could not bear to look on His Body in its glory; we can take it under bread. We could not drink His Blood as His Blood; we can drink it as wine. The form lowers itself to meet us, but what we receive is the same Christ who stands at the right hand of the Father.

From this Chrysostom presses his hearers to a sober reverence. The chalice that receives our lips, he tells the Antiochenes, has held the Blood of God. To approach it carelessly is to court the judgment Paul names in First Corinthians. The same Eucharist that is medicine to the prepared soul is fire to the unprepared. Examine yourselves, he urges his people, and so come.
notes: Chrysostom's eucharistic realism is one of the foundations of Orthodox sacramental theology. The same teaching runs unbroken through Cyril of Jerusalem, John of Damascus, and the later Byzantine commentators.

The closing call to self-examination is liturgically embedded in the prayers of the Hours of Preparation and the Anaphora of the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, which Orthodox Christians still pray each Sunday.
